### C1.11 Regulated FS lens (POV 2)

**Model risk.**
- *SS1/23.* PRA SS1/23 covers vendor models and requires ongoing performance monitoring [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-PRA-SS123: PRA Supervisory Statement SS1/23 'Model risk management principles for banks' (published with PS6/23) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S008: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks (Bank of England / PRA) <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. The gateway is where model-version changes become visible: a provider's silent model update or a fallback event is a change to the "model" that monitoring must detect [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *SR 26-2.* SR 26-2 superseded SR 11-7 on 17 April 2026 and places generative and agentic AI outside its scope [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-US-MRM: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management: Federal Reserve SR 26-2 / OCC Bulletin 2026-13 / FDIC FIL-15-2026 (supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S001: SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (17 April 2026) (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System) <https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.htm> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A8-S002: OCC Bulletin 2026-13 Model Risk Management: Revised Guidance (attachment bulletin-2026-13a.pdf) (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) <https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13.html> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. The firm's own governance must therefore define which routing changes need re-validation [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *Inventory.* Treat each route (purpose, model, fallback, region) as an inventory item linked to C8, not just each model [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**EU AI Act.**
- *Deployer logging.* Article 26 requires deployers of high-risk systems to keep logs for at least six months, folded into financial-services documentation for financial institutions [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-EUAIA: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S011: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EUR-Lex / Official Journal of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Annex III duties apply from 2 December 2027 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-EU-OMNIBUS-AI: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 ('Digital Omnibus on AI') amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, 2018/1139 and 2023/1230 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S011: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EUR-Lex / Official Journal of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].
- *Gateway logs as evidence.* The gateway is the one place that sees every request with its model version, so its logs are the natural Article 26 evidence base, joined to L9 traces [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Most asset-management uses are not Annex III, but the same logs serve MRM and outsourcing evidence [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**DORA, UK CTP and outsourcing.**
- *Third-party registers.* Under DORA, every ICT third-party arrangement belongs in the register of information, with Article 30 terms and exit strategies for critical or important functions [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S021: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) pages and RoI reporting FAQ (ESMA / EBA / EIOPA) <https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. A SaaS gateway (Cloudflare, Portkey SaaS) is such an arrangement [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *Designations.* The DORA CTPP list and the UK CTP designations include AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft, and no AI model provider [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S021: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) pages and RoI reporting FAQ (ESMA / EBA / EIOPA) <https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; R-UK-CTP: UK Critical Third Parties regime (FSMA 2023 / FSMA 2000 s312L; PRA/FCA/BoE CTP rules) and the Critical Third Parties (Designation) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/777) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S023: The Critical Third Parties (Designation) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/777); BoE/FCA/HMT announcements (HM Treasury / legislation.gov.uk / Bank of England) <https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/777/made> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Hyperscaler gateways therefore sit under designated providers; direct model APIs do not [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *Exit planning.* SS2/21 expects documented, tested exit plans, including stressed exit [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-PRA-SS221: PRA SS2/21 'Outsourcing and third party risk management' (revised by PS7/26, March 2026) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S048: SS2/21 Outsourcing and third party risk management (and PS7/26, March 2026) (Bank of England / PRA) <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/-/media/boe/files/prudential-regulation/supervisory-statement/2021/ss221-march-21.pdf> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. The regulatory fact base's own assessment of SS2/21 names the gateway, portable prompts and evaluation suites as the exit route [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The gateway is what makes a model exit a configuration change rather than a code programme; an exit plan that has never been drilled through the gateway is not tested [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *Notification lead time.* PS7/26 and FCA PS26/2 require notification of material third-party arrangements from 18 March 2027 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-PRA-SS221: PRA SS2/21 'Outsourcing and third party risk management' (revised by PS7/26, March 2026) (see regulatory_facts.json); R-FCA-SYSC8: FCA Handbook SYSC 8 (Outsourcing); FG16/5 'Guidance for firms outsourcing to the cloud and other third-party IT services'; PS26/2 operational incident and third-party reporting (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S062: PS7/26 Operational incident and third-party reporting (PRA) and FCA PS26/2; revised SS2/21 (March 2026) (Bank of England / PRA; FCA) <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2026/march/operational-incident-and-third-party-reporting-policy-statement> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Adding a new model provider behind the gateway may itself be such an arrangement, so the gateway's "add provider" change must route through third-party risk [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *Effective access.* FG16/5 expects data location, effective access and exit planning for outsourced IT [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-FCA-SYSC8: FCA Handbook SYSC 8 (Outsourcing); FG16/5 'Guidance for firms outsourcing to the cloud and other third-party IT services'; PS26/2 operational incident and third-party reporting (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S049: FCA Handbook SYSC 8.1; FG16/5; Reporting material third party arrangements (Financial Conduct Authority) <https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/sysc8/sysc8s1> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; that applies to gateway logs held by a vendor [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Resilience: the gateway as a single point of failure.** Concentrating every AI call in one component improves control and worsens resilience [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The answer is not to remove the gateway but to deploy it like payments infrastructure: two independent deployments, tested failover, a defined degraded mode, and an incident classification under DORA's ICT incident regime [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S021: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) pages and RoI reporting FAQ (ESMA / EBA / EIOPA) <https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]] [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Residency and transfers.** EU-to-US transfers rely on the Data Privacy Framework or SCCs, and the C-703/25 P appeal is pending [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DATA-TRANSFERS: UK GDPR as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; EU adequacy decisions for the UK (GDPR and LED); EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S053: Case C-703/25 P Latombe v Commission (appeal against T-553/23) (EUR-Lex / Court of Justice of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/6610/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Processing location is already a priced API control on at least one first-party model API [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A8-S036: Data residency (Claude Platform docs) (Anthropic) <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/data-residency.md> accessed 2026-10-07]; OpenRouter offers EU/US in-region routing on higher plans [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A4-S109: OpenRouter Docs: In-Region Routing (EU/US) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OpenRouterTeam/docs/main/guides/features/in-region-routing.mdx> accessed 2026-10-07]. The gateway is where region pinning is enforced and evidenced per request [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Gateway logs are themselves personal data and must stay in region [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Concentration and ownership.** Palo Alto Networks now owns both Portkey and Protect AI within Prisma AIRS [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A7-S014: Palo Alto Networks Completes Acquisition of Protect AI <https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/company/press/2025/palo-alto-networks-completes-acquisition-of-protect-ai> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A7-S016: Palo Alto Networks Inc Form 10-Q for quarter ended 30 April 2026 (Palo Alto Networks / US SEC) <https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001327567/000132756726000015/panw-20260430.htm> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Stripe has agreed to acquire OpenRouter, with closing pending as of 8 October 2026 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — V1-S059: Stripe agrees to acquire OpenRouter to help businesses optimize token routing and usage <https://stripe.com/newsroom/news/stripe-agrees-to-acquire-openrouter> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]; V1-S060: Stripe to buy OpenRouter as fintech expands deeper into AI (and TechCrunch 16 Aug 2026 report) (CNBC / TechCrunch) <https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/19/stripe-openrouter-fintech-ai-model-marketplace-.html> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]]. IOSCO flags concentration risk from reliance on a few AI technology providers [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-INTL-AI-ASSETMGMT: IOSCO Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets (FR/02/2026) and ESMA Public Statement on AI and investment services (30 May 2024) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S058: IOSCO FR/02/2026 Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets (May 2026) <https://www.iosco.org/library/pubdocs/pdf/IOSCOPD823.pdf> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. A gateway owned by a model vendor, a payments company or a security vendor is not neutral; that matters most for the component meant to keep you neutral [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Security standards.**
- *OWASP.* The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 (released August–September 2026) is the operative list [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-LLM: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (superseded by the OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026) (see regulatory_facts.json); V2-S056: OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 (with press release 'OWASP GenAI Security Project Unveils 2026 Top 10 for LLM Applications, New Agent Control Standard', URL dated 2 <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]]; its full 2026 list was not retrieved. For traceability, the 2025 identifiers the gateway most directly addresses are LLM10 Unbounded Consumption (limits and budgets), LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure (DLP hooks) and LLM03 Supply Chain [R]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Reported — A8-S040: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-llm-applications-2025/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. The Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 starts with ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-AGENTIC: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S042: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (launched 9-10 December 2025) (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; per-caller tool exposure at the gateway limits what a hijacked agent can reach [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *NIST and ISO.* NIST AI 600-1 and ISO/IEC 42001 provide the control taxonomy and management-system wrapper [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-NIST-AIRMF: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1) and Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S044: NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; NCCoE agent identity concept paper; CAISI agent security <https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; R-ISO-42001: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems; ISO/IEC 42005:2025 AI system impact assessment; ISO/IEC 42006:2025 requirements for AIMS audit and certification bodies (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S045: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems <https://www.iso.org/standard/42001> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].
- *ESMA.* ESMA expects ex-ante input controls and frequent ex-post output controls [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-INTL-AI-ASSETMGMT: IOSCO Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets (FR/02/2026) and ESMA Public Statement on AI and investment services (30 May 2024) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S059: ESMA Public Statement on AI and investment services (30 May 2024) and 2026 briefings <https://www.esma.europa.eu/document/public-statement-ai-and-investment-services> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; the gateway is where both are invoked [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

### C1.12 Worked-example slice (POV 3)

**What the commentary agent needs from C1 [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.** The deterministic workflow drafts the monthly Brinson-style attribution commentary (allocation, selection, currency) for a generic multi-asset fund. Every model call it makes goes through the gateway:
1. **One route, one identity.** The workflow calls a named route, `attribution-commentary-draft`, with its workload identity (C4). It never holds a provider key.
2. **Model routing with a residency constraint.** The route's primary model is served from an approved UK or EU region. The route will not send data anywhere else, even under load.
3. **A qualified fallback model.** The fallback is a different provider in the same approved region, and it has passed the same L9 regression suite of past commentaries. If both are unavailable, the route fails closed and the analyst is told the draft is delayed; no unqualified model is tried.
4. **Per-commentary cost attribution.** Each request carries tags for fund, period, commentary ID and workflow version, so C6 reports cost per commentary and per fund.
5. **Inline guards.** Pre-call: DLP on client identifiers (C3) and a prompt-attack check on retrieved documents (C2). Post-call: the numeric-grounding guard (C2) before the draft reaches the reviewer.
6. **Tool access through the gateway's MCP endpoint.** The workflow sees only the read-only attribution-engine tool and the retrieval tool; write tools are not exposed to this caller.
7. **Evidence.** The request record (route, model and version, region, fallback flag, tokens, cost, guard outcomes, trace ID) goes to L9 and to the C8 evidence pack, retained under the records policy and in region.

**What C1 must never do [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:**
- fall back to a model outside the approved region, or to one that has not passed the route's regression suite
- serve a cached draft or paragraph from another fund or period (semantic cache is off on this route)
- let budgets or guards fail open because a dependency is down
- forward the workflow's token to an upstream tool server
- accept a provider-side model version change without recording it and triggering re-qualification
- become the place where drafting logic or numbers are generated; it routes and records, it does not author

### C1.13 Original → current → recommended

**Provisional recommendation.** Split L2 into model serving, inference optimisation and model access [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Promote the gateway out of L2 into the control plane as C1, renamed "AI traffic gateway" to cover model, tool and agent calls, with C2, C3, C4 and C6 invoked through it [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Draw it as a logical control that may be implemented on the firm's API-management platform, not as a mandatory separate product [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Keep agent logic out of it [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. **Provisional; verdict in synthesis.**


## C2. Guardrails

> **Executive summary.** Guardrails are the run-time checks that sit on either side of a model or agent call: they inspect what goes in (user input, retrieved documents, tool results) and what comes out (text, tool calls), and they block, transform or flag it against policy [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The original graphic has no guardrail control; its only safety-adjacent tiles are the L9 evaluation and red-teaming tools, which test before release but block nothing at run time [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A1-S062: Promptfoo README (Promptfoo (OpenAI) (GitHub)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/promptfoo/promptfoo/main/README.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A1-S068: DeepEval README (Confident AI (GitHub)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/confident-ai/deepeval/main/README.md> accessed 2026-10-07] [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Three things define the market in October 2026. First, the hyperscalers now ship broad managed services: Bedrock Guardrails covers content and prompt-attack filters, denied topics, PII, contextual grounding and Automated Reasoning [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07]; Azure Prompt Shields has been GA since August 2024, with Task Adherence for agent tool use in preview [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S055: What's new in Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/whats-new.md> accessed 2026-10-07]; and Google's Model Armor enforces data residency by default [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S067: Model Armor product page (incl. pricing) (Google Cloud) <https://cloud.google.com/security/products/model-armor> accessed 2026-10-07; B-C2-S003: Model Armor: Data residency and endpoints (Google Cloud) <https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/data-residency> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]]. Second, the open-source options are fragile: NeMo Guardrails is still 0.x Beta [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S003: nemoguardrails - PyPI JSON metadata (Python Package Index) <https://pypi.org/pypi/nemoguardrails/json> accessed 2026-10-07], Meta has released no new Llama Guard, Prompt Guard or LlamaFirewall since May 2025 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S006: llamafirewall - PyPI JSON metadata (Python Package Index) <https://pypi.org/pypi/llamafirewall/json> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S107: Llama Guard 4 model card; Llama Prompt Guard 2 model card; Llama Protections (Meta) <https://developer.meta.com/ai/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama-guard-4/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], and Harvey announced its acquisition of Guardrails AI on 9 September 2026, after the project had retired hosted remote inference [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S028: Guardrails AI Joins Harvey <https://www.harvey.ai/blog/guardrails-ai-joins-harvey> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; V2-S026: Guardrails AI Joins Harvey (with Artificial Lawyer 9 Sep 2026, The Next Web, unite.ai) <https://www.harvey.ai/blog/guardrails-ai-joins-harvey> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]; V2-S071: Guardrails HUB_UPDATE.md (Guardrails AI (Harvey)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/guardrails-ai/guardrails/main/HUB_UPDATE.md> accessed 2026-10-08]. Third, guardrails are moving towards agent behaviour, checking tool use and goal hijacking [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S055: What's new in Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/whats-new.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S039: LlamaFirewall README (GitHub) (Meta) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/meta-llama/PurpleLlama/main/LlamaFirewall/README.md> accessed 2026-10-07]. **Recommendation:** own the guardrail policy and its test set; invoke guardrails from the gateway (C1) as a layered set of deterministic rules, small classifiers and, only where needed, model-based checks; and remember that a guardrail cannot make an autonomous workflow safe that should have been a deterministic one (L3) [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

### C2.1 Responsibility

**The problem this control owns.** At run time, stop inputs and outputs that breach policy, and record why [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. It breaks down into six jobs:

- **Input controls.** Detect prompt injection and jailbreaks in user input and, more importantly for agents, in retrieved documents and tool results (indirect injection) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Azure Prompt Shields covers both user-input and document attacks [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S054: What is Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/overview.md> accessed 2026-10-07].
- **Output controls.** Block or transform harmful, off-policy, leaking or ungrounded output [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- **Policy enforcement.** Denied topics, word lists, regulated-advice restrictions and house rules [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07] [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- **Content safety.** Harm categories with thresholds [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S054: What is Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/overview.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S067: Model Armor product page (incl. pricing) (Google Cloud) <https://cloud.google.com/security/products/model-armor> accessed 2026-10-07].
- **Grounding checks.** Is the output supported by the supplied context, and are its numbers the authoritative ones? [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07] [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}
- **Agent-behaviour checks.** Is the agent's tool use aligned with the task? Azure Task Adherence (preview) and LlamaFirewall AlignmentCheck target this [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S055: What's new in Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/whats-new.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S039: LlamaFirewall README (GitHub) (Meta) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/meta-llama/PurpleLlama/main/LlamaFirewall/README.md> accessed 2026-10-07].

**Three kinds of mechanism [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.** The distinction matters for latency, cost, explainability and false positives:

| Mechanism | Examples | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Rules** (deterministic) | Word filters, denied-topic lists, regex and entity patterns, numeric comparators | Fast, explainable, brittle; false positives are predictable and fixable |
| **Classifiers** (small trained models) | Prompt Guard 2 (22M/86M), Llama Guard 4 (12B), Prompt Shields, content filters | Fast to moderate; probabilistic; thresholds need tuning per domain and language |
| **Model-based judges** (an LLM checks the output) | NeMo self-check rails, LlamaFirewall AlignmentCheck (chain-of-thought auditing) [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S036: NeMo Guardrails CHANGELOG.md (NVIDIA) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails/develop/CHANGELOG.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S039: LlamaFirewall README (GitHub) (Meta) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/meta-llama/PurpleLlama/main/LlamaFirewall/README.md> accessed 2026-10-07] | Flexible, slow and costly; can be manipulated by the same text it judges; needs calibration |

Bedrock's Automated Reasoning checks sit apart from all three as a formal-reasoning check [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07]; its exact mechanism was not reviewed in the fact base [NPV]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Hand-offs.** C2 is invoked by the gateway (C1) before and after model and tool calls, and by the workflow (L3) at its own checkpoints [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. It shares PII detection with C3 (C3 owns tokenisation and residency; C2 owns blocking) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. It shares detectors and attack datasets with L9 (offline red-teaming) and C7 (security testing) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Its decisions feed C8 evidence [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**What the control does not own.** It does not own the decision about how much autonomy a workflow has (L3), the authorisation of tool calls (C4), or the validation of output quality over time (L9) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

### C2.2 Why it matters

**Guardrails cannot fix a workflow that should never have been autonomous [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.** This is the central design point for this control. A guardrail is a filter on a stream of actions; it reduces the probability that a bad action passes, but it does not reduce the number of actions an agent is allowed to attempt. If an agent has write access to a client-facing system, a content filter on its output is not a control over that access [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The plan's worked example is built as "a deterministic workflow, not a free agent", with read-only tools and a human approval gate; most of its safety comes from that design, and the guardrails are the second line [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The OWASP Agentic list starts with ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-AGENTIC: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S042: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (launched 9-10 December 2025) (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], and the most effective mitigation for goal hijack is to give the agent no goal it can be hijacked towards: fixed steps, read-only tools, scoped identity [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

When guardrails are badly designed, four things go wrong [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:
- **Wrong place.** Only the user's prompt is screened, while retrieved documents and tool results, the real injection path for agents, pass unchecked.
- **Wrong mechanism.** A content-safety classifier is asked to catch a business error it was never trained for, such as a wrong sign on a currency effect.
- **False positives drive bypass.** An over-sensitive filter blocks legitimate finance vocabulary, users route around it, and the control disappears.
- **Fail open.** A guard times out and the gateway passes the request.

**Illustrative scenario [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.** A fund-reporting workflow retrieves a broker's market note to add context to the monthly commentary. The note's PDF contains text in a white font: an instruction to describe the fund's currency effect as positive and to omit the selection effect. The firm's guardrails screen the analyst's request for jailbreaks and the model's output for harmful content and PII. Neither check fires: the analyst's request is benign, and the output is polite, harmless and contains no personal data. The draft goes to the portfolio manager with a reversed currency effect and a missing paragraph. It is caught only because the numeric check in L9 compares each figure and direction word with the attribution engine output. Afterwards the team adds two controls: a prompt-attack check on every retrieved chunk before it enters the prompt, and the same deterministic numeric comparator inline as a blocking output guard, not only as an offline evaluation. The scenario is invented; it is not a reported incident.

### C2.3 Goals and KPIs

| KPI | Definition | Target guidance [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"} | How it is measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attack catch rate | Share of red-team attack cases (OWASP LLM and Agentic 2026) blocked or flagged | No critical misses at release; tracked per attack class and language | Red-team suite in CI (L9), replayed against the live guardrail configuration |
| False-positive rate | Share of a labelled benign set (real, approved finance text) blocked | Set per route; e.g. below 1% for drafting routes | Benign regression set run on every threshold or version change |
| Indirect-injection coverage | Share of retrieved chunks and tool results screened before entering a prompt | 100% for external or third-party content | Gateway and workflow logs |
| Numeric grounding pass rate | Drafts whose figures and direction words all match the authoritative source | 100% to release; any miss blocks | Deterministic comparator, inline and in L9 |
| Added latency | p95 latency added per guard and per route | Budget per route (e.g. small classifiers in tens of milliseconds; judges only where justified) | Guard spans in the trace |
| Guard cost per 1,000 requests | Unit cost of all guards on a route | Visible to C6; reviewed quarterly | Vendor unit prices times guard volume |
| Fail-closed conformance | Guard failures (timeouts, errors) that let a request through | 0 on regulated routes | Chaos tests; guard outcome logs distinguishing block from failure |
| Override and tuning trail | Threshold changes and overrides with approver and reason | 100% recorded | C5 change log |
| Bypass detection | Calls that reach a model without passing the route's guards | 0 | Gateway coverage reconciliation (C1) |

### C2.4 How it works

Guardrails are a pipeline of checks placed at four points [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:

1. **On input**, before the prompt is assembled: user request screening (jailbreak, policy), PII handling via C3.
2. **On context**, before retrieved documents and tool results enter the prompt: prompt-attack screening of each chunk. Prompt Guard 2 has a 512-token window [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S030: meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B model card and LICENSE (Hugging Face); Llama Prompt Guard 2 model cards (Meta (via Hugging Face)) <https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], so long documents must be chunked before screening [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
3. **On output**, before the response leaves: harm categories, PII leakage, policy topics, grounding against context, and deterministic business checks.
4. **On action**, before a tool call executes: alignment of the call with the task. Azure Task Adherence (preview) detects misaligned or premature tool use [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S055: What's new in Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/whats-new.md> accessed 2026-10-07]; Foundry guardrails can inspect tool calls and tool responses (preview), but only for Foundry Agent Service agents [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S103: Guardrails and controls overview in Microsoft Foundry <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/guardrails/guardrails-overview> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Authorisation of the call itself belongs to C4 [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

Each check returns allow, block or transform. NeMo Guardrails' IORails engine formalises this as an engine-neutral `RailOutcome` contract and distinguishes policy blocks from rail execution failures [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S036: NeMo Guardrails CHANGELOG.md (NVIDIA) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails/develop/CHANGELOG.md> accessed 2026-10-07]. That distinction is what lets a route fail closed on errors without treating every error as a policy event [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Where the checks run.** Guardrails can run inside the application (library), as a sidecar or server, or as a managed service invoked by the gateway. The gateways all expose hooks: LiteLLM runs guardrails pre-call, during the call or post-call across chat, embeddings, MCP and A2A routes [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S015: LiteLLM docs: MCP Overview, Agent Gateway (A2A), Caching, Budgets/Rate Limits, v1.89.0 release notes (BerriAI (LiteLLM)) <https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/mcp> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; Kong integrates AWS, Azure and GCP guardrail services and NeMo Guardrails [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S017: Kong AI Gateway changelog; Kong Gateway changelog; AI Proxy Advanced plugin docs (Kong Inc.) <https://developer.konghq.com/ai-gateway/changelog/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; APIM applies Content Safety to MCP tool-call arguments and A2A payloads [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S020: Azure API Management AI gateway docs and Tech Community announcements (AI Gateway tier preview; Build 2026 updates) (Microsoft) <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/ai-gateway-overview> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; Apigee calls Model Armor inline [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S024: Apigee AI solutions: gateway to enterprise-ready AI (Google Cloud) <https://cloud.google.com/solutions/apigee-ai> accessed 2026-10-07]. Bedrock's `ApplyGuardrail` API applies Bedrock policies to content from any model [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S073: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock runtime (botocore service-2.json) - ApplyGuardrail (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock-runtime/2023-09-30/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07].

```text
 user request ─► [input rules + jailbreak classifier] ─┐
                                                       ▼
 retrieved docs / tool results ─► [chunk ─► prompt-attack classifier] ─► prompt assembly (L3)
                                                                              │
                                                       gateway (C1) ─► model (L1/L2)
                                                                              │
 output ◄─ [deterministic business checks: numbers, signs, terms] ◄─ [harm / PII / topic / grounding] ◄┘
   │            (rules: block on any mismatch)              (classifiers; judge only where needed)
   ▼
 human review (L3 gate) ──► release        every outcome ─► trace (L9) ─► evidence (C8)
 proposed tool call ─► [task-alignment check] ─► C4 authorisation ─► tool (L4)
```

**Latency and cost.** Every guard adds both, and they stack [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The unit economics differ by mechanism:

- Small classifiers are cheap: Prompt Guard 2's 22M variant is designed for low-latency, low-compute use, while Llama Guard 4 is a 12B model needing GPU-class serving [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S030: meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B model card and LICENSE (Hugging Face); Llama Prompt Guard 2 model cards (Meta (via Hugging Face)) <https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].
- Managed services price per volume: Bedrock bills per 1,000 text units per configured policy (content filters and denied topics US$0.15, sensitive-information filters US$0.10, Automated Reasoning US$0.17, as of 7 October 2026) [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S101: Amazon Bedrock Pricing (Guardrails); Guardrails reduces pricing by up to 85% (Dec 2024); Safeguard tiers (June 2025) (Amazon Web Services) <https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; Model Armor is free to 2M tokens a month, then US$0.10 per 1M tokens [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S067: Model Armor product page (incl. pricing) (Google Cloud) <https://cloud.google.com/security/products/model-armor> accessed 2026-10-07]; Azure Content Safety bills per 1,000 text records per model, a record being up to 1,000 characters, and its S0 unit prices could not be verified [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S102: Content Safety in Foundry Control Plane - Pricing; Azure AI Content Safety FAQ (Microsoft) <https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/content-safety/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A6-S054: What is Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/overview.md> accessed 2026-10-07]; Cloudflare's guardrails are billed as Workers AI inference [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S052: Cloudflare AI Gateway docs: Pricing (source mdx) (Cloudflare, Inc.) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cloudflare/cloudflare-docs/production/src/content/docs/ai-gateway/reference/pricing.mdx> accessed 2026-10-07].
- Model-based judges cost a model call each and add the most latency [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

Route-level design follows: deterministic rules everywhere, small classifiers on all untrusted input, managed or larger classifiers on output, and model-based judges only on routes where nothing cheaper can decide [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

### C2.5 Enterprise design principles

**Security**

- Screen indirect inputs (retrieved documents, tool results, emails), not only user prompts [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack is the first entry in the OWASP Agentic list [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-AGENTIC: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S042: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (launched 9-10 December 2025) (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].
- Fail closed on regulated routes. NeMo's streaming output rails fail closed when actions fail (0.24.0) [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S036: NeMo Guardrails CHANGELOG.md (NVIDIA) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails/develop/CHANGELOG.md> accessed 2026-10-07]; LiteLLM's prompt-injection guardrails are off by default [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S015: LiteLLM docs: MCP Overview, Agent Gateway (A2A), Caching, Budgets/Rate Limits, v1.89.0 release notes (BerriAI (LiteLLM)) <https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/mcp> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Configure and test the behaviour explicitly [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Do not let one model judge itself. A judge that reads attacker-controlled text can be attacked by it [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Do not rely on one detector family. An independent tester reported Prompt Guard weak against non-English and obfuscated prompts [R]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Reported — A6-S031: Sharing new open source protection tools and advancements in AI privacy and security; Llama Protections page (Meta) <https://ai.meta.com/blog/ai-defenders-program-llama-protection-tools/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Layer classifiers from different vendors and include multilingual cases in the test set [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Scalability, resilience and cost**

- Give each guard a latency budget and a timeout, with a defined outcome on timeout [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Run cheap checks first and stop early on a block [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- A managed guardrail service in a different provider or region from the model adds a dependency and a data flow; include it in the resilience and residency analysis [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Governance and false-positive management**

- Version guardrail configurations, thresholds and detector versions in C5, and record which version made each decision [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Maintain two datasets: an attack set (OWASP-mapped, multilingual) and a benign set of real approved text from the domain. Every threshold change runs both [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Provide a governed override path: an analyst can request release of a blocked draft, a second person approves, and the case joins the benign set if it was a false positive [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Without that path, users find their own bypass [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Classify each guard's decisions as policy blocks or execution failures, so failures are fixed and blocks are reviewed [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S036: NeMo Guardrails CHANGELOG.md (NVIDIA) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Guardrails/develop/CHANGELOG.md> accessed 2026-10-07] [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Observability**

- Emit each guard decision (guard, version, score, threshold, outcome, latency) as a span on the request trace (L9) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- Watch block rates per route; a sudden rise is either an attack or a regression in the guard [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Portability**

- Keep the policy (what is forbidden, and on which route) separate from the detector (which product detects it) [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Then a vendor change swaps detectors without rewriting policy [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Patterns [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:** guardrails invoked from the gateway; layered rules → classifiers → judges; screening of every retrieved chunk; deterministic business checks as blocking output guards; benign and attack regression sets; governed overrides; policy separate from detector.

**Anti-patterns [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:** guardrails as a substitute for workflow design; screening only the user prompt; a content-safety classifier as the only output check for a numbers-heavy document; LLM-as-judge for checks a regex or comparator can do; thresholds tuned once on vendor defaults; silent fail-open on guard timeout; a guardrail service outside the approved region for client data.

### C2.6 Product selection criteria

| Scorecard criterion | What to evaluate in this control [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"} |
|---|---|
| Technical (15% FS) | Coverage of input, indirect-input, output, grounding and tool-use checks; which mechanisms (rules, classifiers, judges); multilingual performance on your data; configurable thresholds; block vs transform; standalone API usable from any gateway |
| Enterprise readiness (15%) | Identity and audit on configuration changes; versioned configurations; support |
| Security and compliance (20%) | Certifications naming the service; CMK; fail-closed behaviour; for self-hosted, release hygiene and licence clarity |
| Deployment flexibility (15%) | Self-hosted or in-region managed service; residency enforcement of guard inference |
| Ecosystem (5%) | Gateway integrations (LiteLLM, Kong, APIM, Apigee); framework integrations |
| Reliability and maturity (10%) | GA vs preview; release cadence; ownership stability; maintenance risk |
| Cost / TCO (5%) | Unit price per policy and per volume; GPU cost for self-hosted classifiers; judge-token cost |
| Lock-in / portability (15%) | Proprietary API vs open weights or open source; whether policies can be expressed outside the vendor |

**Scoring notes [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:**

The three managed services (Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety, Model Armor) are Strategic, conditional, "where this is your primary cloud" under rubric rule 10 (CP3 Q2): each is its cloud's lead guardrail service and none has a criterion at 1. No criterion scores changed, and security stays at 4 under rule 8. The firm's own guardrail policy, its attack and benign test sets, and the gateway hooks that invoke detectors are still the durable asset; the detectors behind them should stay substitutable, which is why the open-source frameworks remain Tactical.
- *Hyperscaler presumption (CP2 Q1).* Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety and Model Armor score 4 on enterprise readiness: platform controls presumed (CP2 Q1); confirm per service.
- *Scope rule (CP2 Q4).* Bedrock Guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety score 4, not 5, on security because their certifications are stated for Bedrock or Azure without naming the guardrail service (B-C2-S001, B-C2-S002, B-C1-S007, B-C1-S008). Model Armor is named in Google's scope but CMK is not verified, so 4.
- *Rule 2 (self-hosted software and open weights).* NeMo Guardrails, Guardrails AI and the Llama Protections are scored as software you run, so the NPV cap does not apply. NeMo has commercial support through NVIDIA AI Enterprise; the other two have none verified.
- *Rule 3 (ownership change).* Guardrails AI's lock-in is reduced by 1: Apache-2.0, but owned by an application company rather than a neutral body.
- *Maturity of the managed services.* Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety and Model Armor all score 3. ### C2.9 Decision tree

```text
STEP 0 [Rec] (not optional): decide the workflow's autonomy FIRST (L3).
  Can the task be a deterministic workflow with read-only tools and a human gate?
  ├─ Yes → build it that way; guardrails are the second line
  └─ No  → document why; tool authorisation (C4) and approval gates come before guardrails

STEP 1 [Rec]: Deterministic checks (always, in-house)
  Business invariants (numbers, signs, terms, forbidden phrases, identifiers) → rules/comparators
  coded by the firm, run inline as blocking output guards and in L9 CI

STEP 2 [Rec]: Managed or self-hosted detectors for injection, harm and PII?
  Where does the model run?
  ├─ AWS          → Bedrock Guardrails (Classic tier / region-pinned for client data) via ApplyGuardrail
  ├─ Azure        → Azure AI Content Safety (Prompt Shields on user input AND documents) via APIM
  ├─ Google Cloud → Model Armor (strict residency on, EU template) via Apigee
  └─ Multi-cloud or in-estate required →
        NeMo Guardrails server (pinned) orchestrating:
          Prompt Guard 2 (22M) on every retrieved chunk  +  a second, independent detector
          (a managed service above, or Check Point AI Guardrails, C7)

STEP 3 [Rec]: Model-based judges?
  Only where no rule or classifier can decide (e.g. tone, policy nuance); never as the sole
  check on numbers; calibrated against human labels (L9) before it blocks anything

STEP 4 [Rec]: Agent tool use
  Tool calls → C4 authorisation (deny by default) first;
  task-alignment checks (Azure Task Adherence, LlamaFirewall AlignmentCheck) only as extra signal

STEP 5 [Rec]: Checks before go-live
  Attack set (OWASP LLM and Agentic 2026, multilingual) and benign set both passed?
  Guards fail closed on timeout? Guard inference in the approved region? Override path governed?
```

### C2.10 Lock-in classification

| Element | Classification [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"} | Rationale | Abstraction to use [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"} |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guardrail policy (what is forbidden, per route) | **Unacceptable if held only in a vendor console** | It is the firm's control statement and validation evidence | Policy as code in Git (C5), referencing detectors by role |
| Detector product (classifier or managed service) | **Acceptable** | Detectors are substitutable if called through the gateway | Gateway guard hooks (C1); per-detector adapters |
| Managed guardrail APIs (Bedrock, Azure, Google) | **Manageable** | Proprietary APIs, but policies are simple to re-express [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S054: What is Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/overview.md> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S067: Model Armor product page (incl. pricing) (Google Cloud) <https://cloud.google.com/security/products/model-armor> accessed 2026-10-07] | Standalone API calls from the gateway rather than model-coupled configuration |
| Open weights under community licences | **Manageable** | Portable, but licence terms and maintenance are risks [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S030: meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B model card and LICENSE (Hugging Face); Llama Prompt Guard 2 model cards (Meta (via Hugging Face)) <https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A6-S107: Llama Guard 4 model card; Llama Prompt Guard 2 model card; Llama Protections (Meta) <https://developer.meta.com/ai/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama-guard-4/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]] | Record licence; keep a second detector |
| Attack and benign test sets | **Unacceptable if only in a vendor tool** | They are what lets you swap detectors safely | Git-versioned datasets shared with L9 and C7 |

### C2.11 Regulated FS lens (POV 2)

**Model risk.**
- *SS1/23.* SS1/23 includes model risk mitigants (Principle 5) and ongoing performance monitoring [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-PRA-SS123: PRA Supervisory Statement SS1/23 'Model risk management principles for banks' (published with PS6/23) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S008: SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks (Bank of England / PRA) <https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Guardrails are mitigants; their own false-positive and false-negative rates must be monitored like model performance [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. A classifier or judge used as a guardrail is itself a model and belongs in the inventory [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
- *SR 26-2.* SR 26-2 places generative and agentic AI outside its scope and leaves their governance to the firm's own practices [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-US-MRM: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management: Federal Reserve SR 26-2 / OCC Bulletin 2026-13 / FDIC FIL-15-2026 (supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S001: SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management (17 April 2026) (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System) <https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.htm> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A8-S002: OCC Bulletin 2026-13 Model Risk Management: Revised Guidance (attachment bulletin-2026-13a.pdf) (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) <https://www.occ.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2026/bulletin-2026-13.html> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Guardrail standards are therefore set by the firm [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Supervisory expectations.** ESMA expects "ex-ante input controls and frequent ex-post output controls" for AI in investment services [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-INTL-AI-ASSETMGMT: IOSCO Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets (FR/02/2026) and ESMA Public Statement on AI and investment services (30 May 2024) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S059: ESMA Public Statement on AI and investment services (30 May 2024) and 2026 briefings <https://www.esma.europa.eu/document/public-statement-ai-and-investment-services> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Input guardrails are the ex-ante control and output guardrails plus L9 online evaluation are the ex-post control [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. UK supervision relies on existing frameworks, including SM&CR accountability and Consumer Duty outcomes [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-UK-AI-STATEMENTS: FCA, Bank of England and PRA statements and initiatives on AI, 2024-2026 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S055: FCA announces second cohort for AI Live Testing (April 2026); FS25/5; Mills Review (Financial Conduct Authority) <https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/fca-announces-second-cohort-ai-live-testing> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; a named owner for guardrail policy fits that model [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**EU AI Act.** Article 26 requires deployers of high-risk systems to monitor operation and keep logs for at least six months [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-EUAIA: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S011: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EUR-Lex / Official Journal of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], with Annex III duties from 2 December 2027 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-EU-OMNIBUS-AI: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 ('Digital Omnibus on AI') amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, 2018/1139 and 2023/1230 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S011: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EUR-Lex / Official Journal of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Guardrail decisions (what was blocked, by which version) are part of that log [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Article 50 transparency has applied since 2 August 2026 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-EUAIA: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S011: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EUR-Lex / Official Journal of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; guardrails do not substitute for the disclosure duty [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Operational resilience and outsourcing.** A managed guardrail service on the request path is an ICT third-party dependency for DORA's register [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S021: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) pages and RoI reporting FAQ (ESMA / EBA / EIOPA) <https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]] [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. If it is down, the route fails closed and the business service degrades, so its availability belongs in the impact tolerance analysis [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The hyperscaler guardrail services sit under providers designated as CTPPs and UK CTPs [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DORA: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S021: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) pages and RoI reporting FAQ (ESMA / EBA / EIOPA) <https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; R-UK-CTP: UK Critical Third Parties regime (FSMA 2023 / FSMA 2000 s312L; PRA/FCA/BoE CTP rules) and the Critical Third Parties (Designation) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/777) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S023: The Critical Third Parties (Designation) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/777); BoE/FCA/HMT announcements (HM Treasury / legislation.gov.uk / Bank of England) <https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/777/made> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].

**Residency.** Guardrail inference processes the same client data as the model. Bedrock's Standard tier uses cross-region inference [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07; A6-S101: Amazon Bedrock Pricing (Guardrails); Guardrails reduces pricing by up to 85% (Dec 2024); Safeguard tiers (June 2025) (Amazon Web Services) <https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]; Model Armor enforces residency by default but has conflicting statements for London [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — B-C2-S003: Model Armor: Data residency and endpoints (Google Cloud) <https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/data-residency> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]; B-C2-S005: Model Armor release notes (Google Cloud) <https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/release-notes> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]]. EU-to-US transfers rely on the Data Privacy Framework or SCCs, with an appeal pending [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-DATA-TRANSFERS: UK GDPR as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; EU adequacy decisions for the UK (GDPR and LED); EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/1795) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S053: Case C-703/25 P Latombe v Commission (appeal against T-553/23) (EUR-Lex / Court of Justice of the EU) <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2025/6610/oj/eng> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Run guardrails in the same approved region as the model, or in-estate [Rec]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Auditability.** Each decision needs the guard, its version, score, threshold, outcome and any override with approver [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. Overrides are the most important records: they show that humans, not filters, made the final call [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Concentration and ownership.** Guardrail vendors are being absorbed: Check Point bought Lakera [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A7-S012: Check Point to Acquire Lakera, Redefining Security for the AI era (Check Point Software) <https://blog.checkpoint.com/security/check-point-to-acquire-lakera-redefining-security-for-the-ai-era/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; A7-S013: Check Point Software Technologies Completes Acquisition of Lakera to Secure the World's AI Transformation (CXOtoday (republished Check Point press release)) <https://cxotoday.com/press-release/check-point-software-technologies-completes-acquisition-of-lakera-to-secure-the-worlds-ai-transformation/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], Palo Alto Networks bought Protect AI [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A7-S014: Palo Alto Networks Completes Acquisition of Protect AI <https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/company/press/2025/palo-alto-networks-completes-acquisition-of-protect-ai> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], and Harvey bought Guardrails AI [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S028: Guardrails AI Joins Harvey <https://www.harvey.ai/blog/guardrails-ai-joins-harvey> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Meta's open components have not been updated since May 2025 [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S107: Llama Guard 4 model card; Llama Prompt Guard 2 model card; Llama Protections (Meta) <https://developer.meta.com/ai/docs/model-cards-and-prompt-formats/llama-guard-4/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. A two-detector design from different owners is a concentration control as well as a security one [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.

**Standards.**
- *OWASP.* The Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026 (August–September 2026) is operative [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-LLM: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (superseded by the OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026) (see regulatory_facts.json); V2-S056: OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026 (with press release 'OWASP GenAI Security Project Unveils 2026 Top 10 for LLM Applications, New Agent Control Standard', URL dated 2 <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/> accessed 2026-10-08 [search-tool extract]]; its full list was not retrieved. For traceability, the 2025 identifiers most relevant to guardrails are LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM05 Improper Output Handling and LLM09 Misinformation [R]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Reported — A8-S040: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-llm-applications-2025/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. The 2026 edition is reported to rank Excessive Agency third [R]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Reported — A8-S041: OWASP GenAI Security Project Unveils 2026 Top 10 for LLM Applications, New Agent Control Standard <https://genai.owasp.org/2026/09/01/owasp-genai-security-project-unveils-2026-top-10-for-llm-applications-new-agent-control-standard-and-sponsors-as-community-tops-30000-members/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]], which is an L3 and C4 design issue that guardrails only partly mitigate [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}. The Agentic list's ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-OWASP-AGENTIC: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S042: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 (launched 9-10 December 2025) (OWASP GenAI Security Project) <https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]] is the threat that indirect-input screening addresses.
- *NIST and ISO.* NIST AI 600-1 lists GenAI risks and suggested actions; ISO/IEC 42001 provides the management-system wrapper [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — R-NIST-AIRMF: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1) and Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S044: NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile; NCCoE agent identity concept paper; CAISI agent security <https://www.nist.gov/publications/artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-generative-artificial-intelligence> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]; R-ISO-42001: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems; ISO/IEC 42005:2025 AI system impact assessment; ISO/IEC 42006:2025 requirements for AIMS audit and certification bodies (see regulatory_facts.json); A8-S045: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 AI management systems <https://www.iso.org/standard/42001> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]].

### C2.12 Worked-example slice (POV 3)

**What the commentary agent needs from C2 [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.** The deterministic workflow drafts the monthly Brinson-style attribution commentary (allocation, selection, currency) for a generic multi-asset fund, and calls its guards through the gateway route `attribution-commentary-draft`:
1. **Client identifiers.** Before any text reaches the model, C3 tokenises client names, account numbers and personal identifiers; a C2 PII guard on output blocks any identifier that slips through. Bedrock's PII filter covers UK NI and NHS numbers, IBAN and SWIFT [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07]; firm-specific account formats need the firm's own patterns [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}.
2. **Prompt injection from retrieved documents.** Every retrieved chunk (prior commentaries, house style, approved market notes) is screened for prompt attacks before it enters the prompt, using a document-attack detector such as Prompt Shields [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S054: What is Azure AI Content Safety? (Microsoft Learn source) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs/main/articles/ai-services/content-safety/overview.md> accessed 2026-10-07] or Prompt Guard 2 on 512-token chunks [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S030: meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B model card and LICENSE (Hugging Face); Llama Prompt Guard 2 model cards (Meta (via Hugging Face)) <https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-Guard-4-12B> accessed 2026-10-07 [search-tool extract]]. Third-party market notes get a second detector. A flagged chunk is dropped and logged, not sanitised.
3. **Numeric grounding check.** A deterministic comparator extracts every figure, sign and direction word ("added", "detracted", "overweight") from the draft and checks that each appears in, and agrees with, the attribution engine output for that fund and period. Any figure not in the attribution output, or any mismatch outside the agreed rounding rule, blocks the draft. This is the same check L9 runs offline, run inline here as a guard.
4. **Narrative grounding.** Market-context sentences must be supported by approved retrieved sources; a contextual-grounding check (e.g. Bedrock's [VF]{custom-style="Claim Label"}^[Verified fact — A6-S072: AWS API model: Amazon Bedrock control plane (botocore service-2.json) - guardrail shapes (Amazon Web Services (via boto/botocore)) <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boto/botocore/develop/botocore/data/bedrock/2023-04-20/service-2.json> accessed 2026-10-07]) flags unsupported claims for the reviewer rather than blocking.
5. **Policy topics.** Denied topics: forward-looking return forecasts and personal recommendations; the draft is commentary, not advice.
6. **Fail closed.** If any guard times out, the draft is held and the analyst is told; nothing is released unchecked.
7. **Evidence.** Each guard decision, version and override is written to the trace and the C8 evidence pack.

**What C2 must never do [AJ]{custom-style="Claim Label"}:**
- let a model-based judge override a failed deterministic numeric check
- treat "all guardrails passed" as approval; the human approval gate (L3) remains mandatory
- send client data to a guardrail service outside the approved region
- silently sanitise an injected document and continue as if it were trusted
- be used to justify giving the workflow more autonomy or write access than the deterministic design needs
